title.narrative: 1.4.1B. Forestry network members have access to nearreal time forest data for forestry monitoring and protection.

description.narrative: 18 maps based on satellite imagery have been produced from the Forest Canopy Disturbance Monitoring (FCDM) tool developed by EU Commissions Joint Research Centre and introduced to community members. The maps helped the community members understand how the total forest cover has changed over the last few years. Some community members noted that the map could even allow them to use it for education in the community and the public. All the maps are marked yearly; however, each yearly file contains both semester files for each wildlife sanctuary. Our Future Organization has received a thirdparty grant and Prey Lang app training; additional maps have been created for the Phnom Tnout Phnom Pok Wildlife Sanctuary. As a result, more maps than expected have been produced.

description.narrative: According to the Facebook Analytics tool, CCIMs Environmental Justice Facebook page has reached more than 3 million people, with at least 6375 (1833 Females and 4,737 youths) engagements over the course of the year for overall content posted on the page. 3,207 people (827 women, 2076 youth) engaged directly via monthly the Radio Talk Show, and 3168 people (1006 women, 2661 youth) engaged with the contents of the Environmental Justice page. title.narrative: Intermediate Outcome 2(IO2). Forest dependent community members are more engaged in socially inclusive protection of natural resources.

description.narrative: As a result of CEEJA activities, FCDMs are more engaged and involved in forest protection; they care about forests and want to protect them. Female FCDMs have used the knowledge acquired to access resources and overcome social barriers to engagement in environmental justice. PFCN and PLCN two of the important forestry networks supported by CEEJA are encouraging community members and network members, including women and youth, to protect their forests and NFTPs, e.g., resin trees. Together with PFCN, PKH has also supported several traditional groups (1,066 members, 473 women, 477 IPs) to protect and conserve the Prey Preah Rokar forest. PFCN has worked closely with these groups and encouraged them to engage more in forest protection. If FDCMs observe forest crimes while collecting NTFPs, they now report these to PFCN, which is a behaviour change. PKH has also supported communities to participate in coordinated campaigns for policy and law enforcement; 491 community members (227 women, 161 IPs, and 191 youth) participated. The joint campaigns were organized in conjunction with the International Day of Forests, World Environment Day, and others. Moreover, they also posted and shared content about these events on their Facebook page to seek more participation from community members and Cambodian citizens at large. In addition, two other third parties (Environment and Health Education Organization (EHE) and Highlanders Association (HA) have supported community members to improve their livelihoods and participate in forest protection. Finally, PBO has helped female FCDMs to apply the knowledge acquired when addressing local conflicts and NRM issues.

title.narrative: Intermediate Outcome 1(IO1). Youth, in particular young women, become leaders in advocating for equitable governance of natural resources.

description.narrative: CCIM has engaged youth through its SoMe platform and by engaging with this platform, youth have demonstrated their considerable interest in environmental justice issues. Youth trained by CCIM have continued their SoMe activities and have been a good source of information on local matters for CCIM when reporting on environmental issues. CYN has conducted training for youth and forestry network members on natural resource management, forestry law, protected area law, public speaking, negotiation skills, and constituency building. The training has enabled forestry network members to better understand their rights and advocate for equitable governance of natural resources. CYN has supported youth to increase their commitment to engage in forest protection. DAN has provided training to forestry network members, including youth, on using the Prey Lang app and drones. The training has benefited youth to collect data on biodiversity and forest crimes and monitor the protected forests status. PBO has empowered female youth to engage more in community activities, e.g., recording biodiversity in their forests. PKH has observed that youth actively support activities of forestry networks, for instance, evidencebased research on forest crimes and forest land encroachment.

title.narrative: 1.2.3.Young female forest guardians enhance their skills to defend their natural resources.

description.narrative: CYN has trained 15 people (11 women, 6 IPs) in fundamental rights and advocacy to help them better understand their roles, rights, and responsibilities regarding environmental protection. PBO has completed the Peace KASH, conflict resolution and transformation training for cohort 2. Twentythree (23) women (18 from PLCN and 5 from PFCN) have graduated and started to apply the training. PBO has continued to provide ongoing support and coaching for the 23 women so they can address community issues, e.g., mediating conflicts. As a result of this support, the women are more confident in supporting their community, including dealing with violence against women and children. Some women have participated in forest patrols and fish conservation. Some women are now able to deal with and overcome alcohol addiction and address their family problems more peacefully. title.narrative: 1.1.2.Urban and rural youth, and forest dependent community members are connected in support of environmental justice.

description.narrative: CYN organized an exposure visit with 30 participants (18 women) to MCF in Sorng Rukhavoan Wildlife Sanctuary. University students, community members, and monks met and discussed deforestation, illegal logging, and biodiversity. They also went on forest patrol together. The youth created videos, posters and wrote poems about the monks efforts to protect the forest and shared them on their social media accounts. CYN also provided training on constituency building for community members and youth in Steung Treng with 15 participants (11 women). The training included fundamental human rights, protected area law and forestry law, negotiation, and public speaking skills. Furthermore, CYN organized a leadership camp in the Kbal Khla community forest in Kampong Thom with 30 participants (18 female youth). The camp brought university students, community members, and local youth together to learn about youth leadership, environmental impact assessments (EIA), environmental rights, participation in the development process, and Indigenous Peoples rights. CYN produced and shared a video about the camp on social media. The CYN activities helped youth and community members to connect for future collaboration and mutual support. Ten (10) youth (6 women, including 1 IP) joined the Youth Fellowship Program with CYN, and they stayed in communities in Preah Vihear, Kampong Thom, and Steung Treng. The fellowship program provided space for urban youth, especially university students, to learn facilitating skills, internet security, GPS usage, nonviolation communication, advocacy skills, and report writing. The youth learned more about the experience of FDCMs from living and working with them in the communities, searching and documenting forest issues, including community livelihoods. Youth and FDCM developed a solid relationship to share and exchange information about social problems and environmental justice activities.

title.narrative: STO1.3.Forestry networks have greater capacity and voice to assert their rights to natural resources.

description.narrative: CYN trained 132 people (65 women) in Kratie, Steung Treng, Preah Vihear, and Kampong Thom on fundamental human rights, a rightsbased approach, advocacy, and situation analysis. Representatives from MoE participated in the training, which is considered an achievement given the current state of relations between civil society and government. Forestry network members applied the training when advocating for better protection of and access to their forests. Importantly, PLCN members have noted improvements in their project planning capacity and awareness of their rights to participate in forest protection. As a result, they have: 1) issued statements expressing their concerns about deforestation, 2) raised concerns about forest crimes when interviewed by radios and newspapers, 3) engaged in dialogue with relevant authorities, and 4) organized joint forest monitoring visits. CEEJA does not cover any administrative expenses of PLCN. MCF community members have also improved their ability to raise awareness of forest issues and their forest protection activities. The forestry network members (FNMs) who received Prey Lang app training said they were able to use it to collect data on forestrelated crimes. As a result of PBO efforts, there has been improved family reconciliation, community solidarity, and better advocacy for protecting their forests (Prey Lang and Prey Preah Rokar). PKH has witnessed forestry network members being more motivated and engaged in forest conservation and protection. For instance, the FNMs now report immediately to PFCN when observing forest crimes while collecting NTFPs.

title.narrative: 1.4.2A. Forest dependent community members are enabled in forestry monitoring and customary usage of biodiversity.

description.narrative: DAN has provided Prey Lang app training to 109 FDCMs (62 from PLCN, 22 from PFCN, 15 from MCF, and 10 from OFO). The training has enabled FDCMs to collect data about biodiversity, forest crimes, climaterelated events, and threats while conducting forest patrols and collecting NTFPs. As a result, the trained participants engaged their members to join forest patrols. 30 members of, Kbal Khla. 52 members of MCF members, 41 members of PLCN, 32 members of PFCN were enabled to join the forest patrols. The data has been analysed by the Forest & Peoples Organization and compiled into a monitoring report and extracted for research by the University of Copenhagen (UCPH). Nonsensitive data have been uploaded to IFOROS and are available to FDCMs, FNMs, and the general public. Some third parties, PFCN, MCF, OFO, and Kbal Khla, have used the grant to organise communitybased monitoring and collect data. All data can be viewed at https://iforos.live/platform. Select the layers of preference by pressing the layers tab (upper left corner). To see (nonsensitive) data collected from communities, select the layers Community patrol data. Subsequently, press on the colourful dots on the map to see detailed observations of the entries recorded. FN members also record data on threats and violence, as well as luxury trees and their locations, which are classified as sensitive data by the communities. Through the support of PFCN, 491 participants (227 women, 161 IPs, and 191 youth, 1 commune councillor, 13 MoE/DoE/Forest Ranger Official) have been engaged in forest monitoring through organising collective campaigns for policy improvement and enforcement (forest law, protected area law, environmental code). The participants posted and shared content on Facebook and engaged independent media with their messages. The key messages were: rights to natural resource and customary rights, protect Preah Roka forest from promoting IP culture, protect Preah Rokar to encourage community economically, protect Preah Roka to save human beings and wildlife, etc.

title.narrative: 1.2.1A. Young women minimize opportunity costs to participation in forestry justice activities.

description.narrative: PKH has supported 155 community members (99 women, 99 youth, 134 IPs) to engage twice in the CDP and CIP processes. They suggested that councillors should include ecological farming, irrigation, ponds, etc., in the CDPs and CIPs to improve their livelihoods. The commune councillors promised to take the input from the community members to the district authorities and other stakeholders. Whether this will result in women accessing incomegenerating activities remains to be seen. The women are monitoring this to see if support will be provided. PKH also facilitated 43 leaders from IPAFS groups (42 women, 36 IPs, 20 youths and 1 commune councillor) to learn and share best practices on ecological farming and home gardening. PKH has provided a grant of USD 678 to ten IPAFS groups and provided training on management, roles and responsibilities to group members. The groups are practising ecological farming and home gardening for food consumption. Based on a case study of one family in Brame (Indigenous village) the family earned 500.000 Riels (over six months) from selling vegetables, chickens, and ducks. In addition, community members from the IPAFS groups earned 630,548.00 Riels from selling NTFPs and agricultural products during Womens Environmental Defender Exhibitions (1.2.2 below) at the Weekend Market and in their villages. PKH also organised discussions with 29 NTFP members (6 women, 9 IPs, 4 youth), including resin and honey groups from villages around Preah Rokar Wildlife Sanctuary, on sustainable NTFP collection and market of NTFP products. They identified the current local price of NTFP; for example, the resin price is 80,000.00 Riels per container, and the price of wild honey is 55,000.00 Riels per litter on average. They also discussed the value chain of products and market price from producers to endusers and its prices. Moreover, they also learned to negotiate a better price with buyers.

title.narrative: STO1.2. Young women become more capable and committed to serve as environmental defenders.

description.narrative: Several related outcomes have supported women to become more able to serve as environmental defenders. CCIM has provided grants to 3 young female journalists to write indepth articles on environmental topics, published on the VOD website and SoMe platforms. Young female journalists have also assisted in environmental reporting during field trips. Women trained by CEEJA have joined VOD talk shows as guest speakers discussing various topics related to womens participation in forest protection. CYN has provided capacity building to women for their empowerment and has observed that some of them then started engaging in NRM issues. PBOs training helped raise awareness of the importance of the role of young women in protecting their forests. PBO also connected them with local activists. This will enable them to identify other young women from their community and beyond to join and be more active in protecting their forest. PKH organized a womens forum and observed that 90 people (84 women, 63 IPs, 38 youth) were involved in sharing concerns on environmental justice issues. Moreover, PKH supported 155 people (99 women, 99 youths, 143 IPs) to provide input to the Commune Development Plan (CDP) and Commune Investment Program (CIP). They suggested including forest patrols, awarenessraising and reforestation in the CDP and CIP. The commune councillors shared their input at a district integration workshop to call for support from other stakeholders. Finally, ten IPAFS groups led by women (and supported by PKH) have organized exhibitions and set up stores in Preah Vihear provincial town and their villages/communes. In total, 121 (119 women, 121 IPs, 68 youth) were involved.

title.narrative: 1.2.2.Young women benefit from networking and support to develop their role as guardians of the forest.

description.narrative: Three (3) female journalists received story grants from CCIM. They wrote indepth articles on environmental justice issues that were published on the VOD website, VODs Facebook page, and the Environmental Justice page. Moreover, CYN supported two youth groups (65 women) in networking and information sharing. As a result, these female youth groups were able to organize a campaign for the International Day of Forests in Phnom Penh and Prey Lang and a youth dialogue in Phnom Penh. The activities contributed to raising awareness of environmental justice issues. PBO provided ongoing support and coaching to 24 graduated female peacebuilders (PLCN: 19, PFCN: 5) and supported them to plan community initiative events, including mobilizing local and external resources to support their efforts. PKH organized womens forums in which 89 community members (84 women, 63 IPs, 38 youth) shared their knowledge and experience of natural resource management issues and food sovereignty. They discussed illegal logging and forest encroachment in the Prey Preah Rokar forest. They also exchanged experiences of protecting the forest and shared best practices on ecological farming, home gardening and animal raising, plus womens saving groups. Moreover, they developed action plans to put these ideas into practice. As mentioned in 1.2.1 above, 105 members (103 women, 105 IPs, 55 youth, 105 FDCMs) of IPAFS groups joined exhibition events. The IPAFS members advocated for public support of their traditional Indigenous products through the exhibition. They presented the food systems, agriculture products, and NTFP products to advocate for food sovereignty and rights to access resources. They also posted and shared content on social media to promote their products. The key messages were: having forest is having NTFPs, having land is having agricultural products, please grow the crops that we eat and eat the crops that we grow, promoting local products to improve community economies and promote organic products from local communities.

CCIM has observed that female youth are less inclined to engage in issues that are regarded as sensitive. CYN has noted that youth have become more aware of environmental justice issues, have shared more news about forests and the environment on social media, and have become more creative in promoting environmental rights. Youth have also created groups on social media to share information about social and environmental issues. PKH has observed an increase in youth using the Prey Lang app to record data on biodiversity and forest crimes. As an example, PKH observed that youth were not so active in community forestry protection work to begin with. title.narrative: Expected Impact(EI): Citizens and civil society organisations are empowered to innovate peaceful practices and promote inclusive policies for access to environmental justice.

description.narrative: While it is still too early to report achievements in the expected impact, significant progress has nevertheless been made. CCIM has reached more than 3 million people and engaged more than 130,000 people on issues related to environmental justice through its SoMe platform. Forestdependent community members have increased their ability to effectively report on environmental issues, contributing to more awareness of those issues. CYN has continued to create spaces for university students and local community youth to discuss the impacts of deforestation on the environment. CYN has provided digital security training for female frontline activists. They have dedicated time to apply the new learning by participating in forest crime investigations and sharing news about these events on social media. The female activists of CEEJA have also advocated for environmental justice, especially at the local level, and used their rights as citizens to engage in forest protection. Youth and community members have produced several reports on forest crimes. The subcontractor Forest & Peoples Organization has finalized the creation of the IFOROS platform. This systems data on biodiversity and forest crimes has authored several forest updates on these events within three protected forests of Prey Lang, Prey Preah Rokar, and Sorng Rukhavoan. The forest updates and data are also publicly available on the Environmental Justice page. They aim to promote inclusive policy dialogue at the local, national, and international levels concerning environmental justice. Some forestry network members have been able to access the protected forests to monitor forest crimes and collect data. The monitoring has been conducted jointly with forest rangers in a few instances. PBO has strengthened and improved community solidarity and nonviolent advocacy on the part of women for forest protection and more engagement of female youth in community activities such as communitybased monitoring. PKH has empowered forestry network members and forestdependent community members (FDCM) to collect data on forest crimes and biodiversity using the Prey Lang app and GPS (data feeds into IFOROS). With this data, the FDCMs have been able to advocate for better forest protection, become more efficient in sharing news on social media and improve their negotiations with local authorities for better forest access. With the support of PKH, the Monk Community Forestry (MCF) network has cooperated with local authorities and civil society actors to raise public awareness of its forest protection work. PKH has supported the Indigenous People Agriculture Farming System (IPAFS) group members to practise ecological farming, home gardening, animal raising, and organizing exhibitions to promote NFTP and agricultural products.
